variants.name: java.util.concurrent.Flow / Reactive Streams demand protocol
variants.idiom_name: Flow.Publisher/Subscriber + Subscription.request(n) (or bounded BlockingQueue for threads)
variants.implementation_notes: Java encodes backpressure as a protocol: java.util.concurrent.Flow (JDK 9, semantically 1:1 with the Reactive Streams specification) has the Subscriber request n items through its Subscription, and a conforming Publisher must never emit more than the outstanding demand, so the consumer's capacity is the signal and buffers stay bounded on both sides. The classic queue-plus-blocking-producer structure is not written by hand: SubmissionPublisher (or a reactive library) implements the mechanics, and the Subscriber only decides how much to request (a small initial demand re-requested as items are consumed, e.g. half the buffer). Where a protocol is overkill - plain threads - a java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue with a fixed capacity gives the same bound: put() blocks when full, offer(timeout) bounds the wait, and put on an overloaded stage becomes the explicit stall.
pitfalls: request(Long.MAX_VALUE) is unbounded demand: the API stops protecting you, and a publisher may accumulate or emit without a consumer-sized bound; request only what can be handled.
Blocking inside onNext (JDBC, file I/O, Thread.sleep) stalls the publisher's thread and silently breaks the demand protocol; hand work to a bounded executor instead.
Executors are the hidden unbounded queue in most Java services: a fixed thread pool with a LinkedBlockingQueue accepts unlimited tasks, so the source is never told to slow down.
A Subscription must be requested from onSubscribe before any item can arrive, and request(-1) is a spec violation that terminates the flow.

variants.name: Project Reactor / RxJava operators (Java 8)
variants.implementation_notes: On Java 8 the same demand protocol is supplied by a library rather than the JDK: Project Reactor and RxJava implement Reactive Streams, and operators are the policy surface - onBackpressureBuffer(n) bounds a local buffer and applies its configured overflow action when full; it does not make an already-unbounded upstream wait. Use limitRate or a naturally demand-aware source when pacing is required, and use onBackpressureDrop/onBackpressureLatest only when shedding is semantically valid. flatMap(..., concurrency) limits in-flight work. The classic structure is replaced by the operator that owns the queue, so the design work moves to choosing finite capacity, overflow policy and concurrency instead of writing a queue; when the source is cold and pull-based (Flux.fromIterable, generate) backpressure is structural, and none of the onBackpressure* operators are needed at all.
pitfalls: Operators that accept unbounded demand (onBackpressureBuffer() with no capacity, publish().onBackpressureBuffer(), or an unreviewed flatMap prefetch/concurrency) can recreate an unbounded queue; use finite capacity and configure concurrency explicitly.
Mixing blocking calls into a reactive chain holds the operator's thread and destroys the demand signal; wrap them in boundedElastic/subscribeOn with a bound.
onBackpressureDrop/Latest silently discard data - correct for telemetry, wrong for messages whose loss must be visible.
A hot shared publisher (Sinks.many().multicast()) is paced by its own buffering, not by the slowest subscriber, so per-subscriber backpressure must be added explicitly.

variants.name: Virtual threads with bounded blocking queues (Loom)
variants.idiom_name: ArrayBlockingQueue capacity + blocking put on virtual threads
variants.implementation_notes: With virtual threads (JDK 21) the blocking form becomes the idiomatic one again: an ArrayBlockingQueue or LinkedBlockingQueue with a fixed capacity, plus a thread per request/handler, gives real backpressure because the blocked virtual thread costs almost nothing and unmounts from its carrier while waiting. The classic producer/consumer structure is unchanged - the queue and the blocking put - but the cost model that made callback/reactive flow control necessary disappears, so the simpler form is often the better engineering choice. The bound must be enforced on the queue (ArrayBlockingQueue capacity, Semaphore, or a bounded executor) because Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a new thread per task and therefore bounds nothing.
pitfalls: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() bounds nothing by itself: without a bounded queue or semaphore a slow consumer still gets an unbounded backlog of virtual threads.
Blocking on a bounded queue is only backpressure if the producer path is the one blocking; an intermediate executor re-introduces an unbounded hand-off.
synchronized blocks that pin the carrier (long-lived native/FFI sections) turn cheap blocking into platform-thread starvation.
Queue bounds must be sized against the downstream's real concurrency budget; a 100k-capacity queue just delays the failure and blows the latency target.
